Meta's gearing up for a stock sale.

On Monday, Meta launched a plan to raise up to $95 billion in stock, upsized Tuesday to $97.5 billion. Naturally, Nvidia and AMD, two of Meta's biggest chip suppliers, said they were buying. Nvidia would invest $3 billion and AMD $1 billion. Just 96% of the raise to go as the circle in circular finance continues to spin.

Meta carried about $115 billion in debt and lease obligations as of September 30, per its quarterly filing, within $206.45 billion in total liabilities. Its future commitments dwarf both. Bloomberg reported on October 22 that Meta's lease and contract commitments hit about $825 billion, up from nearly $700 billion in July. That total includes $355.7 billion in leases not yet on the balance sheet, per the filing. Nikkei Asia put the figure at $420 billion in late July.

Capex keeps climbing on top of that. Meta narrowed its 2026 guidance last week to $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the floor and implying $49 billion to $59 billion in Q4 spending alone. The combined weight likely forced Meta's hand: it issued more stock.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

At the same time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he would help Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg out with $3 billion, the companies said. Meta plans to deploy more Nvidia Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs to support Muse, Meta's AI agent. Muse launched last month and is third on the U.S. free iPhone chart as of October 26, behind Vinted, a secondhand store app, and TikTok Pro. It's ahead of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

The good thing about issuing new common shares is Meta doesn't have to pay anything back or pay interest. That said, $12.5 billion of preferred pays a 6.5% dividend. The bad thing is shareholders get diluted by about 5.5% if the full plan sells, per a StockTitan estimate. EPS is also going to take a hit if Meta can't pump its profits.

But that's the price Big Tech and the hyperscalers feel is worth paying to guarantee their slice of the AI industry. If they don't grab it now, someone else will.

Wall Street's growing demand for free cash flow is pushing Big Tech to cut costs as AI spending soars, Bloomberg Tech host Ed Ludlow said Wednesday, days after Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) reportedly offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees.

"Wall Street cares about free cash flow now. It really does," Ludlow said on Bloomberg Radio.

He contrasted the stronger stock performance of cash-rich Apple Inc. and Nvidia Corp. with lagging Microsoft, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META).

Companies committing enormous sums to AI infrastructure need a "mechanism for belt tightening," Ludlow argued, with workforce reductions one possible response.

Big Tech's AI Spending Dilemma

Wall Street wants technology companies to invest aggressively in AI, but investors are becoming less tolerant of the cash those investments consume.

That leaves companies facing a difficult choice: find savings elsewhere or risk disappointing shareholders.

Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) has already faced that dilemma. The company slashed its workforce earlier this year, with TD Cowen estimating 20,000 to 30,000 job cuts could free up $8 billion to $10 billion for its AI data-center expansion.

Ludlow said Oracle faced a harsh market reaction when its free cash flow turned negative, while investors were more forgiving of Amazon.

Meta's free cash flow turned negative last quarter, and its headcount fell 15% from a year earlier, its latest results show.

"The market is fickle," he said, arguing that Wall Street judges companies individually.

Even profitable Microsoft faces growing pressure. Its operating cash flow rose 34% last fiscal year, but infrastructure spending grew faster, leaving less cash after investment.

Borrowing is becoming more expensive, too. A separate Bloomberg report Wednesday identified at least 18 data-center financings carrying double-digit yields as lenders grew more cautious about the AI boom.

On Polymarket, traders put roughly 9% odds on a qualifying AI industry downturn by Dec. 31, with $3.1 million in total volume. The contract requires three specified distress events within 90 days.

Why Jobs Are Under Pressure

Microsoft's buyout offers reportedly cover roughly 27% of its workforce, although how many employees will accept remains unknown.

Bloomberg reported that Xbox, Windows, Copilot and finance teams are participating, while some data-center employees are excluded.

title: Mark Zuckerberg's Meta Platforms Reported Negative Free Cash Flow for the First Time Since 2012. Here's Why That Milestone Matters for Shareholders.
detail:
Mark Zuckerberg's Meta Platforms Reported Negative Free Cash Flow for the First Time Since 2012. Here's Why That Milestone Matters for Shareholders.
Neil Patel, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 28, 2026 at 12:50 PM EDT 5 min read
META
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) just gave investors a fresh update on its financial results. During the third quarter, the social media empire reported revenue of $64.6 billion, which soared 26% year over year. This marked the third straight quarter that the top line grew by more than 25%, an impressive feat given how massive the business is.

But the story continues to be how much money Meta Platforms is spending on artificial intelligence (AI) investments. Operating income fell 37%, compressing the operating margin from 40% in Q3 2025 to 20% in the latest quarter.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

And in what was probably an unsurprising development, the company posted negative free cash flow (FCF) of $2.1 billion in Q3. This hasn't happened since 2012, the year that Meta Platforms, then called Facebook, went public. Here's what the FCF milestone means for shareholders.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Management is spending at a breakneck pace

During the third quarter, Meta Platforms' capital expenditures (capex) totaled $34.9 billion, up 80% year over year. This pushed FCF into negative territory, as the business burned $2.1 billion. It's been well over a decade since this has occurred. But given that fellow internet giant Alphabet reported negative FCF in the second quarter, investors must have seen this coming.

Meta Platforms is a hyperscaler. It's sparing no expense to build out AI-related compute capacity, primarily data centers and supporting technical infrastructure. Its capex figures have ballooned. And they are now expected to be $140 billion (at the midpoint) in 2026.

That spending is showing no signs of slowing. As of Sept. 30, Meta Platforms had $825 billion in future commitments, up from $643 billion as of June 30. That huge sum is equal to half of the company's total market capitalization. It's easy to believe this will continue to expand in future quarters.

This is no longer a capital-light enterprise that was printing cash. Meta Platforms has become a capital-intensive business. It's also borrowing to fund the AI build-out. Long-term debt is at $80.9 billion. Exactly four years ago, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT, there was $9.9 billion in long-term debt on the balance sheet.

The consensus view among sell-side analysts is that Meta Platforms will report negative FCF of $10.6 billion in 2026. Next year, FCF will be in the red by almost $35 billion. Then in 2028, it will turn positive again. Take this forecast with a grain of salt, however, as nobody knows how the AI boom will evolve in the coming years.
